cards.title: Whiplash Head Turn
gear: A marker word ("Yes!") or a clicker
steps: Toss a treat a few feet away and say "Get it!" so he knows he can eat it.
As he finishes the treat, before he looks up, say his name.
The instant his head turns back toward you, mark it ("Yes!" or a click) and give a really special reward.
Repeat, tossing a little farther each time as his confidence grows.
Variation: as he grabs one treat, say his name and toss another in a different direction. Keep going until he is racing back and forth.
tips: Timing matters: mark while his head is turning back to you, which encourages the fast turn.
If he loves to run, toss farther so he gets to run more.
Great for energetic dogs; the back-and-forth variation builds excitement for the head turn.
cards.levelUp: He snaps his head back to you quickly, even when the treat is tossed farther away.
cards.source: Mardi Richmond, Whole Dog Journal (2014, updated 2022)

cards.title: Build the Stop Cue
gear: A leash short enough to reach his nose
steps: First decide what Stop means to you. Here: stop what you're doing, come back to me, and get a big reward.
Pick a quiet spot like the living room or kitchen. Keep him on a leash short enough to reach his nose.
Part 1: say "Stop." Right away put a really good treat at his nose.
Keep feeding as you back up a few steps and he follows: 15 treats or more, with warm praise.
Say "All done!" to end. Repeat Part 1 at least 5 times.
Part 2: say "Stop," then pause. The moment he starts to turn toward you, expecting the treats, mark it.
Then give the same treat stream (15 or more) while backing up, and end with "All done!"
Repeat Part 2 at least 10 times, then take a break.
tips: Don't make Stop mean "stop and stay far away". Distance is much harder to train.
Not working? Use better treats. He may be giving up something great to come to you.
Be generous. At least 15 pieces each time, and he decides what is generous enough.
Too exciting? Make the set-up easier.
Use the leash only to keep him from wandering off, never to pull him in.
Toy-size dog: use tiny pieces and count them toward his daily food.
cards.levelUp: He swings toward you the moment he hears "Stop" in the quiet room. Next: Stop, Then Back to Play.

cards.title: Stop, Then Back to Play
gear: Something he loves to go back to: a playmate dog, ball, tug, or dinner
steps: Pick something he really wants to go back to: play with another dog, a ball, tug, chase, or dinner.
Start with low distractions. While he's doing that activity, say "Stop" and give the treat stream as before.
Say "All done!" and let him go right back to what he was doing. That is the second reward.
With another dog, start with both dogs on leash, just looking at each other from at least 10 feet away.
Slowly let play run longer between Stop breaks, and add new toys or more excitement before each Stop.
If he doesn't enjoy that playmate, the break itself is the reward.
tips: Don't jump from living-room practice straight to free play in the yard.
Keep him on a leash or otherwise controlled early on, so you decide how it goes.
If it's too hard to leave the activity, make the set-up less exciting.
No other dog? A ball, tug, or chase works as the "back to play" reward.
cards.levelUp: He breaks off play when you say "Stop," runs to you for treats, then happily goes back. Next: use Stop in real life (door, window, squirrels).
